newsitem.title: USA: Emerging debt rises, tracks U.S. Treasuries.
newsitem.headline: Emerging debt rises, tracks U.S. Treasuries.

text.p: Emerging debt prices rose slightly, as a lackadaisical Brady bond market trailed strong U.S. Treasuries higher, traders said.

A recent flood of sovereign debt issues, coupled with a slowdown typical of summertime and the end of a week, led to a dull day of Brady bond trade, with most dealers awaiting fresh incentive to drive the market.

"Positive sentiment in the U.S. bond has helped Brady bonds," said one Brady bond trader. "There were some new issues to look at this week, which probably took some of the focus off of the Brady market."

In late afternoon trade, Argentina FRBs ARFLC05=RR were unchanged at 94-1/4, while Brazil "C" bonds BR8D14=RR picked up 1/2 to 81-3/4 bid. The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond gained 12/32 to yield 6.65 percent.
"The market definitely has tightened quite a bit, but I haven't seen any real buying," said the chief dealer at one U.S. investment bank. "It's going to be one of those long summers."

Earlier this week, emerging nations, such as Russia, Mexico, Argentina, Philippines and South Africa, took advantage of low rates and a global craving for yield to float more than $5.0 billion of new debt.

"What we're seeing is the fading of the Brady era and the market focus beginning to shift toward newer more dynamic areas," said Thomas Trebat, head of emerging markets research at Citicorp Securities.
The largest deal of the current batch was Russia's $2.0 billion 10-year eurobond priced 375 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries.

"The Russian eurobond was an important development," Trebat said, adding that the issue meant that money managers unable to put their money into Vnesh loans or other existing instruments could now invest in Russian assets.
